parts.visual:
When a company becomes so massive that it destroys all competition, it attracts the attention of 'Anti-Trust' regulators (like the FTC or DOJ in the US).

The Anti-Trust Threats:
1. Blocked Mergers: The government stopping you from buying your biggest rival because it would create a monopoly.
2. Breakups: The government forcing your massive company to split into 3 smaller companies (like Standard Oil or AT&T).
3. Predatory Pricing: Being sued for lowering your prices so much that you bankrupt small competitors.
parts.audio: When a company dominates an entire market, it faces Anti-Trust regulations. The government can block your mergers, fine you for predatory pricing, or force you to break up the company.

questions.question: Your tech giant wants to buy the only other major tech giant in the industry. What will the government likely do?
options: File an Anti-Trust lawsuit to block the merger, arguing that combining the two companies will create a monopoly and harm consumers by raising prices.
Buy shares in the new company.
questions.correct_answer: File an Anti-Trust lawsuit to block the merger, arguing that combining the two companies will create a monopoly and harm consumers by raising prices.
questions.explanation: Governments exist to protect free markets. If one company owns 90% of a market, the market is no longer free.

questions.question: Listen to the government regulator. What illegal tactic is he describing?
questions.tts_text: They intentionally sold their product at a massive loss for three years just to bankrupt the smaller startups. Now that they are the only option left, they tripled the price.
questions.explanation: Using a massive war chest of cash to artificially destroy competition is highly illegal under anti-trust law.

questions.question: If the government decides your company is an illegal monopoly, what is the ultimate 'nuclear' punishment they can inflict?
options: A Forced Breakup. A judge orders your single massive company to be chopped into several smaller, independent companies to create artificial competition.
questions.correct_answer: A Forced Breakup. A judge orders your single massive company to be chopped into several smaller, independent companies to create artificial competition.
questions.explanation: This is the ultimate nightmare for a CEO. It happened to Standard Oil and AT&T, and is a constant threat to modern tech giants.

questions.question: How do executives usually defend themselves against anti-trust claims?
options: They argue that they are not actually a monopoly by defining their 'Market' much more broadly (e.g., 'We don't have a monopoly on smartphones, we just compete in the broader digital entertainment space').
questions.correct_answer: They argue that they are not actually a monopoly by defining their 'Market' much more broadly (e.g., 'We don't have a monopoly on smartphones, we just compete in the broader digital entertainment space').
questions.explanation: Anti-trust law is incredibly complex and subjective. Defining the exact boundaries of the 'market' is how lawyers win these cases.
